09:00.headline: Pitchers: beyond the radar gun
09:00.topic: What college coaches evaluate in pitchers: velo and projection, command, secondary pitch, repeatable delivery

captions.instagram:
Your son throws 84. Is that what college coaches are really looking at?

Velocity gets attention. It's rarely the whole story.

⚾ Velo, and where it's headed as he gets stronger
⚾ Strikes: can he command the zone when it counts?
⚾ A secondary pitch he trusts in any count
⚾ A delivery he can repeat pitch after pitch

A pitcher who fills the zone and is still adding velo can be a better fit for a program than a harder thrower who walks the bases loaded.

Save this before his next bullpen or showcase.

captions.facebook:
Pitcher parents: the radar gun matters, but it's only one line on a coach's notes.

When college coaches watch a high school pitcher, they're usually asking a few questions:
✅ What's his velo today, and how much room does he have to add more?
✅ Does he throw strikes, and can he hit spots when he's behind in the count?
✅ Does he have a second pitch he can trust?
✅ Is his delivery repeatable and under control?

(The 84 on our graphic is a sample reading, not a real player.)

Every coach weighs these a little differently, and fit by level matters as much as any single number.

13:00.headline: His skills video: what to show
13:00.topic: Skills video do's and don'ts for recruiting

graphic.headline: His skills video: *what to show*
items: DO: Lead with his best skills

captions.instagram:
A coach may give his skills video a minute or two. Make it count.

✅ Lead with his best skills, not a long intro
✅ Put the date, his height, weight, grad year and position on screen
❌ Don't make it 10 minutes long
❌ Don't bury it in music and effects

Clean angles, real game speed, and recent footage tell a coach more than a highlight reel set to a song.

captions.facebook:
Off-season is a good time to film or update your son's skills video. A few simple rules help coaches actually use it:

DO lead with his best skills right away. Coaches are busy.
DO put the recording date, height, weight, grad year and position on screen.
DON'T stretch it to 10 minutes. Short and focused tends to get watched.
DON'T add music and effects that get in the way of seeing the swing, the arm or the glove.

A clear, recent, well-labeled video sent with a short email goes a long way.
